remember looking at that bit of paper and going, what's the

thought this looks like the worst use of time. I could be

=== Mentorship 2.0 / What We Can Learn from BJJ Ranking Systems ===

earth am i telling you about this well in bjj you're not
even considered a good grappler until you probably reach
brown or black belt which is eight to ten years of training
yet we get caught up living in a world where we think we can
be a black belt at things that matter in a matter of months
i think bj pen holds the record for the fastest black belt

you could argue that the world of business is infinitely
more complex than the world of jiu-jitsu where you're just
finding different ways to make people submit so although i
don't want to shatter your dreams of laying down on a plane
next year we must realize the reality of becoming great at
something takes a long time i won't lie to you now you could
be the next bj pen but think about months and years not
weeks i'd argue it's easier to become an overnight success

=== Mentorship 2.0 / The Algorithm ===

A lot of people seem to think they know the algorithm and
how it works, but the simplest way to think about it, don't
make content to game the algorithm instead, try to impress
humans. Social media algorithms are complex, but at their
core, they aim to keep users engaged for as long as possible
by showing them content they're most likely to interact
with. Different platforms have unique algorithms, but
generally they follow these principles. One, content
scoring, engagement-based. Algorithms give each post a score
based on expected engagement, the likes, the shares, the
comments, the watch time. The more engagement a post gets
early on, the more it gets pushed out to a wider audience.
Then we could look at two, user behavior tracking. Some
platforms track what you like, comment on, and share. How
much time you spend on each post, which topics, accounts,
and hashtags you interact with the most, although I don't
actually think the hashtags feature is really used that much
anymore. And they definitely know when you're pinching in on
people. You see someone, you see that girl you used to go to
school with, maybe she's had a boob job, I don't know. And
you're going, what's that? And you have a little, oh my god.
The next thing, she's all over your feed. So I've heard. The
algorithms are watching all your movements. They're learning
you. They're learning what you like and how you react to
people you like. And probably number three, ranking and
personalization. Your feed isn't just chronological, it's
personalized based on your past interactions, your
interests, and the type of content you engage with. How much
time you spend on the platform, it knows everything. Then
probably four would be virality and momentum. If a post gets
engagement quickly, it will be pushed harder. High retention
videos, ones that people watch to the end, will get boosted.
That's why some people like to try and game the system
making really short reels with text, but I don't really like
those. Comments and shares carry more weight than just likes
on Instagram and Facebook, and it prioritizes family
-friendly content. Well, actually, they say that meta
prioritizes family-friendly content, but I keep seeing
people die on Instagram. They do say you have to, you know,
this is disturbing, and I always do click on it. But yeah,
even TikTok is extremely AI-driven and learns very fast from
your behaviors. It prioritizes watch time and replays more
than the likes of YouTube. And speaking of YouTube, watch
time and click-through rate are probably the key ones.
Longer videos can perform well if they hold retention
because you get that average view duration. When we look at
X or Twitter, it prioritizes engagement, likes, replies,
retweets. Recency plays a bigger role than on other
platforms because of the time-sensitive nature of tweets. As
I said, there's a few things I hate, and it's people trying
to get the caption to do the work, getting people to watch a
reel over and over as they read the caption. They're trying
to game the algorithm. They think they can use measures like
average view duration or telling people to save a workout.
To be quite honest, I think this is a load of shit. People
communicate and build relationships with people. You walking
on a treadmill with some caption, you'd be like, read the
caption, and the reel doing an average view duration. I hate
it. I think it's cheap. I think it's lazy. I think you can
do better. You should stop doing it.

=== Mentorship 2.0 / Law of Reciprocity ===

another pungent strategic way to get people to buy into our
personal brand is what i call the law of reciprocity i'm not
sure if pungent was the right word to use there but it felt
right so let's just get on with that the law of reciprocity
is a fundamental psychological and social principle that
suggests when someone doing something for us we feel a
natural obligation to return the favor this ingrained sense
of balance and fairness is deeply rooted into human behavior
and plays a crucial role in relationships business marketing
and persuasion at its core reciprocity is what keeps social
interaction smooth and cooperative if a friend buys you a
coffee you'll likely feel the need to return the gesture
next time if someone gives you a genuine compliment you may
feel instinctively to offer them one back this principle
extends beyond personal interactions is widely used in
business and marketing strategies companies often leverage
reciprocity by offering free samples valuable content or
small gifts knowing that customers are more likely to
reciprocate by making a purchase or engaging with the brand
in marketing and sales the law of reciprocity is one of the
most powerful tools for influence giving value first whether
enough free trials educational content or exclusive perks
this creates a subconscious sense of obligation in the
recipient and even though there's no formal contracts
between them to give back most people feel an eternal
pressure to give back in some way this could be through
brand loyalty social media engagement purchasing a product
whatever however reciprocity isn't just about financial
transactions it also influences how we form relationships
build trust because people are more likely to help support
or cooperate with those who have already shown kindness or
generosity towards them this can be seen as networking
leadership and even social media where engaging with others
often leads to increased engagement in return another way i
want you to think about this is what can be described as
accruing goodwill with every single post written video blog
whatever it is we can accrue goodwill another way i want you
to think about it is remember when we spoke about bob the
guy who always puts your bins out for you you never even
asked him to but without question without asking for
anything in return bob just does it for the love of it fast
forward a few weeks you see bob down the road stood at a bus
stop waiting for the bus it's just about to rain and you're
on the way to the shops there's a deep rooted feeling in
your stomach as you pass to pop your head in the window and
say bob let me give you a lift i have time honestly this is
the deep rooted law of reciprocity in action do good for
others and they shall do good to you every post everything
you do on social media is putting the bins out for your
avatar even people with shit marketing have clients because
whether they know it or not they put the bins out so much
for their audience that audience literally message them
direct to find out ways they can do business with them
ultimately we want to help ourselves we want to pay
ourselves we want to earn good money live good lives and fly
our families around the world business class to do this help
others it's the best way to help yourself i promise you

=== Mentorship 2.0 / Abandoned Cart ===

one thing i slept on for years was how many people we could
capture from an abandoned cart secrets so what is it in
digital marketing an abandoned cart refers to when a
potential customer adds item to their online shopping cart
before they leave the website before completing the purchase
this is a common issue in e-commerce with an abandonment
rate between 60 to 80 percent the reasons for cart
abandonment vary but typically include unexpected shipping
costs complicated checkout processes simply getting
distracted marketers combat this with abandoned cart
recovery strategies such as email sequences reminding
customers of their unfinished purchase retargeting ads that
display the abandoned products on other websites or social
media and discount offers or free shipping incentives to
encourage checkout and maybe even just streamline checkout
processes to reduce friction for me this was also a perfect
time to add an autoresponder to anyone that got cold feet
this is good for when people are going to direct to the
sales page which can and will happen just from general
exposure people will check out your stuff now even if you
have someone's email address already you could categorize
these people as super hot leads as they're close to the
point of the sale the email marketing response here could be
to double down on the money-back guarantee or even just to
put their fears at ease and ensure them that they're making
the right decision that means that in marketing every few
campaigns you can just say hey check out what i do by
clicking here some people don't want to do the email part
they want to jump straight into bed so an abandoned car is a
great way to do this and by the way when i say campaign it's
a bit of a marketing slogan so in marketing a campaign
refers to a coordinated series of emails that you can send
to your email address if you're thinking
about who handles abandoned cart sequences your website's e
-commerce platforms like shopify typically has built-in
abandoned cart recovery features email marketing tools like
clavio mailchimp active campaign can integrate with your
store to send abandoned cart emails and third-party apps
also offer abandoned cart recovery with sms push
notifications and the way it works is a user adds an item to
their carp doesn't complete the purchase the e-commerce
platform then detects this and you can go ahead and get rid
of the cart and if the app and triggers an automated
abandoned cart sequence, which could be an hour later, 24
hours later. The email then reminds them of the items left
behind. Amazon do this well, sometimes offering an
incentive. And if integrated, retargeting ads on Facebook
and Google can also show them the abandoned product. If you
use Stripe, Stripe does not send the abandoned cart emails,
but can track incomplete payments. Some e-commerce platforms
like Shopify use Stripe as their processor, but the
abandoned cart recovery is still handed by Shopify. Don't
sleep on abandoned carts. Get one set up and occasionally
fire direct traffic for the purpose of hoping they bounce
and you acquire their email address that way.

=== Mentorship 2.0 / Email Reputations ===

in email marketing reputation is like your credit score but
for sending emails if too many of your emails are ignored
marked as spam or deleted without being opened email
providers like gmail and outlook start to distrust you this
means your future emails are more likely to end up in spam
folders instead of inboxes when it comes to maintaining a
good sender reputation only email people who want to hear
from you never buy email lists never do anything dodgy make
sure that you send valuable content not just constant sales
pitches keep engagement high make it very easy to
unsubscribe if people can't opt out easily instead of
unsubscribing they're going to mark you as spam your
reputation is built on how people interact with your emails
if they engage email providers trust you if they ignore or
report you your email stop reaching people's inboxes if
you're new to email marketing and want to avoid having your
emails marked as spam follow these key steps make sure you
get permission first never send emails to anyone that
haven't explicitly agreed to receive them if you can use
double opt-in where subscribers confirm their email address

=== Mentorship 2.0 / Paid Ad Squeezes, Evergreen Squeezes, Eversqueeze ===

First of all, I need to explain to you why you should all be
trying to dominate organic content before paid ads. Everyone
seems to think they could just buy their way into getting
views, engagement, email addresses through paid ads. Now, if
you can master organic content where you have to let people
in the algorithm push you out wider, it's because you get

setting up the videos. You pretty much become a master in
doing this. So then when you put money behind it, you're
going to do even better. So please don't think of paid ads
as a way to circumnavigate the work you need to do to get
good organic content. Like this, Fast and the Furious 1.
Paul Walker, Vin Diesel, they're doing the drag race. They
hit the NOS. You can't hit the NOS too early. Paul Walker
did that. Now look at him. Rest in peace. Instead, you've
got to Vin Diesel it. You've got to wait to the very last
minute till people think you're never even going to use paid
ads. Then boom, you sponsor a post and you're flying.
Eventually, you're going to find one ad that outperforms
others and you'll delve into why. For instance, for this
course, we figured out that fairly early on in creating the
course, if I said the sentence, if you want to work online,
it did really well. Another weirdly was I said, my friends
used to bully me for making online content. So with that in
mind, we'd replicate other adverts around the same thing
said. Then we create video assets, pieces of content with
squeezes in mind. So then I'd say, if you want to work
online and work remote from Bali, well, you're going to need
a strong day-to-day based people to do it. So your products
too and the services. That's why I put together the online
digital nomad starter kit. So then I'd make another piece of
content based on the feedback that we got. My friends used
to bully me for putting online ads on their content. So then
I'd content every day. Now I buy their dinners and they
don't seem to complain so much. I can't promise that the
people close to you won't judge you for the content you
produce in the old days, but what I can do is promise that I
can remove your 10 X biggest barriers to entry with my short
form checkup course that you can access for free. Give me
your best email address and I'll send it straight over. Now
I know this isn't the content section of the course, but the
reality is for all of us, we should be looking at what is
working within other niches and creators, but also what's
working within our own. Because when we reflect back on our
content, we want to be able to take note of what works, what
works well, then what exceeds expectations. And the same
goes within email marketing. One of those emails may break
the traditional massively outperform others. We need to take
note. Was it a subject line? Was it the raw nature of the
email? Did we put RE in the subject line to make it look
like we were replying? Do we make the font bigger? Did we
just put it all lowercase and say, Hey John, did you want to
do this? We must see trends in other people's email
marketing campaigns, and we should piggyback these to
optimize what we can put cash behind. Because what we can
create is an email marketing machine. That's why we have to
talk about content a little bit. And what I mean by this is
this, the ultimate marketer's dream is something called
ROAS, which is called a return on ad spend. So imagine you
have like a magic vending machine. And every time you put a
dollar in it, it spits out $4 in cash. So this means for
every dollar you spend, you're getting four times back. This
is how return on ad spend works or ROAS. It's a simple
formula. If you take the revenue made from your ads and
divide it by how much you spend on those ads, you'll get the
ROAS. So if you spend a thousand dollars on ads and those
thousand dollars bring you in $5,000, your ROAS is five.
Now, if you're a ROAS, you're less than one, you're losing
money because you're spending more than you're making. A
ROAS of one means you're breaking even. Anything above two
or three can be profitable. And five or higher is usually
great. But this number matters because if your ROAS is too
low, your ads aren't worth running. If it's high, you can
confidently spend more on ads, knowing that you'll get more
back. And it takes the guesswork out of advertising and
helps you make decisions based on actual results, not just
hope. So let's just imagine a world where you spend a
hundred dollars and you get 300 emails. Then over the next
15 days, that equates to a thousand dollars in revenue in
profit. That's a five times ROAS. Ideally, we would want to
ramp up daily spend. Now, what often happens is that two
times the ad spend doesn't always mean double the return.
Because when you have an advert expert on your team, they
carefully dial up and back the spend on campaigns to get the
right amount of squeeze out of it. Imagine you're squeezing
a lemon. There's an optimal amount of squeeze. If you don't
squeeze enough, there's juice left inside, but you don't
want to squeeze it too much because once the juices are out,
you're better off moving on to the next lemon. These can
then run evergreen. They just continue over time. They may
diminish over time. That's fine. We call this advert
exhaustion. Then it's time to find fresh lemons. So if we
can have evergreen adverts or even evergreen pieces of

=== Mentorship 2.0 / What is a Landing Page? ===

A landing page is a single web page designed with one goal
in mind, to get a visitor to take a specific action. Unlike
a normal website which may have multiple pages and
distractions, a landing page is focused and direct, usually
built for things like collecting leads, selling a product or
getting signups. The key difference is that every element of
the page is designed to guide the visitor towards a single
outcome without giving them a bunch of other options to
click on. Now what is it used for? Landing pages are
marketing tools. Businesses use them when they want people
to do something specific. Whether that's buying a product,
maybe unfortunately booking a call, signing up for a
webinar, downloading an ebook or subscribing to a
newsletter. But the newsletter will technically put under a
squeeze. Some people would call that a landing page, I'm
just keeping it top level. So instead of sending potential
customers to a cluttered homepage where they might get lost,
you send them to a page that's laser focused on one message,
one offer and one action. So let's quickly look at how this
differs to a squeeze page. So a squeeze page versus a
landing page, what's the difference? With my course, with
how I teach things, a squeeze page is for collecting emails.
The goal, the only purpose is to capture an email address
and maybe even a name. The design would be ultra minimal, no
distractions, no unnecessary info, no testimonials, just a
clear compelling reason to sign up. The call to action,
almost always just one call to action. Enter your email
address to get whatever it is. Or I sometimes like to say,
please give me your best email address. The traffic source
typically used in ads or maybe pop-ups or links within
content where the goal is to build a list, maybe YouTube,
wherever. For the best practices, keep it short and simple.
Headline, sub-headline, make a promise, some kind of sub
-headline, the email field, call to action button, maybe an
image. Don't need a navigation bar, don't need to give
people an exit option unless you're scarce to your urgency.
Lead with value, make it clear what they're getting in
exchange for their email. Here's an example. A marketing
consultant runs an ad saying, download the seven-step email
funnel that prints money. A squeeze page is just a headline,
an image of the PDF, an email box and a get it now button.
No fluff, no other links. Now, a landing page for broader
marketing goals. The goal could be for selling a product,
maybe booking a call, signing up for a webinar, not just
collecting an email. The design would be more detailed than
a squeeze page. It'll often have multiple sections, maybe
what it is, why they need it, the solutions and
testimonials, maybe even some frequently asked questions.
The call to action is still focused, but it might have
multiple touch points. Sign up now button might be repeated
throughout the page. The traffic sourced would be used maybe
in ads for some direct traffic, mostly in email marketing
campaigns, and usually as a homepage alternative. Now, the
best practices, you're asking for more commitment than just
an email. There could be some social proofs and
testimonials, some case studies or results that help remove
doubt, explainer sections that help build trust and address
objections, single clear call to actions, and they can be
repeated multiple types. For example, a property investment
expert runs an ad saying that there's a guide on how to buy
your first investment property. The landing page would then
explain the benefits, show the testimonials from people that
bought it before, and it'd have a big buy now button. Now,
why do I think you should keep squeeze and landing pages
separate? Well, a squeeze page is a way to keep people
connected. It's designed to be frictionless, it's fast, low
commitment, and only asks for an email. A landing page, on
the other hand, is where you're warming someone up for a
bigger action, like making a purchase, or in some cases,
booking a call. If you try and mix the two, you lose
effectiveness. If you ask for too much on a squeeze page,
opt-ins drop. If your landing page only collects an email,
but doesn't push to the next step, you're wasting the
opportunity to sell or to convert. Now, how they work
together, a perfect funnel often uses both. Because the
squeeze page will put someone into an email marketing
capture, which would then put them into some kind of
nurturing sequence, which will then send them to a different
email. A landing page is further down, where it's going to
send people to direct sales or bookings. It's ready to buy
traffic. So if the goal is to get someone into your world,
start with a squeeze page. If the goal is to convert some
warm traffic into buyers, send them to a landing page. A
landing page is where you send someone to buy your shit. It
should be like an Italian restaurant owner outside his
restaurant. I have my product, which is the restaurant. Now,
hopefully I've got it in the right place on social media.
Now, in the onset, I can't just expect people to come in,
they don't know about it. So I need to go out there and be
proactive, to win people over for my business. Like the
Italian restaurant owner, I'll go out to the street. I will
have my pricing on the menu behind me. And I'll say, hey,
you guys hungry, you should check this out. And they won't
be sure. And they don't really like being sold to us. Say,
hey, look, this is the best pizza in all of Italy. Check out
the menu, have a little look. Some people like to press you
down into sales calls and be over. So I don't think that's
the case. Get people in, let them peruse, let them make a
decision for themselves. If they say no, thanks, have a good
night. I hope you have the best dinner wherever you go. Some
people are going to look and they might not like Italian. It
is not your job to convince them that they should be having
Italian tonight. There are enough people out there that love
Italian food that they will find their way into the
restaurant. And remember, you need to over-deliver as the
owner of a restaurant. You say to them, this is the best
pizza in Italy. The truth is, even if it's not the best
pizza in Italy, if it's damn good pizza, they're not going
to complain. You can't cut corners on a landing page. It's
like what you wear on a first date. People using the wrong
fonts, wrong sizes, shitty colors, bad pictures. You
wouldn't have BO on a first date. So don't skip corners for
this. It's important. And we're going to find out for the
next coming modules.

like A-B split testing and pop-ups to optimize its

results, which makes it popular for marketers, small
businesses, and business owners, anyone that's pretty much
running ads or sending people to a platform they need to
convert people. The way it helps people is if you're running

Leadpages cuts the fluff and keeps visitors focused on one

since so much traffic these days is now coming from phones.

the person away from social media usually email maybe text
which i'm going to look into very soon in more detail then
we want to direct these people to our landing page think
about it it makes no sense to send someone from an email to
social media maybe it would help us bump a few views up on
our social media content but the sole purpose of that
content was to get their email address in the first place
worse yet so many email marketing emails have contact
information for their social media on there that's the last
place you want to send someone from email marketing is to
social media imagine if you host a vsl on youtube you send
me there i'll start watching it then i see a suggestion
video now before you know i'm distracted by that before you
know it i'm 10 videos deep into youtube and i never go back
to your offer when i send you to my landing page i control
what you see and what you experience and i just don't have
that same control on youtube the reason i wanted your email
address was so that i didn't have to compete with everyone
else now here we are the landing page has one purpose for
you to consider buying i don't want anything clickable apart
from that that's why websites often suck because people have
about me contact us faqs all these places to click let's
move us away from the offer usually designed for exploration
menus about pages blog posts product catalogues faqs and
they're there to encourage visitors to browse rather than to

bill i buy an aftershave as a dude you You go to the shop,

=== Mentorship 2.0 / The A/B Split ===

we've spoken about this before but let's just cover off the
ab split testing the cheat code for making more sales
without spending more money if you're running traffic to a
landing page and you're not split testing you're basically
playing darts blindfolded hoping something sticks stop
guessing start testing this is where you take two versions
of a landing page change one thing see which one performs
better maybe it's the headline the call to action the color
of the buy now button yes that can make a difference you
send half your traffic to version a and the other half
traffic to version b keep in mind the platform does this for
you see which converts higher the winner stays the loser
gets binned rinse and repeat because you don't actually know
what works until you test it you might think your landing
page is perfect but what if you think and what actually
works are two very different things your audience might
respond better to a shorter page different headline a bigger
checkout button the data doesn't lie more conversions
without more traffic most people think they need more
visitors to make more money wrong you need to make the most
out of the visitor already have if a hundred people land on
your landing page and only two buy a small tweak could bump
that two people to four people which means you've doubled
your sales without spending an extra dollar on ads everyone
me included thinks they're a genius when they're designing a
landing page but testing keeps you humble you might love a
design but if the data says another version performs better
your opinion doesn't matter so let the numbers decide here's
the deal the more you test the more money you make the
higher your conversion the cheaper your ads become let data
not ego decide what works if you're serious about building
and money making landing page start testing today if not
enjoy leaving stacks of cash on the table while someone else
who does test takes your customers now go set up your first
split test your bank account will thank you later

=== Black Belt Content Mastery / The Dark Side of Social Media Growth ===

growth, when it comes to all things content creation, there

is everybody copies each other and you will have to too. Now
the word I like to use for this is something called
emulation. It just sounds a little bit more fancy, but in
essence, what we should be looking at is all other content
creators at all times, especially competitors, not to copy
or rip off, not to copy their transcript and to read it out,
but to look for things that are working. An example that I
love and I use all the time is to do with Batman. We've seen

Spider-Man, they did three of them. Even think about the
Matrix. The Matrix was such a sick film, but then someone

=== Send Emails, Get Paid / Autoresponders vs Broadcast ===

I know when I say autoresponders or I say broadcast, neither
of them are really going to make much sense to you. But
think about it this way. I've got 10,000 people on an email
list. I can do one of two things. I can send them an email
right now. Hell, I might even email everyone in the
mentorship that's not bought from me today and say, hey,
today I went to the gym and I recorded a brand new email
marketing course. I've been quite vague with the name
because I haven't actually decided yet. Usually I would have
picked this first, but I like the idea of calling this
write, send, sell, but you never know. So because of that,
and I've got the data, I can broadcast to those people, but
just broadcasting to people can put a lot of stress on me
because let's say I'm really busy for the next week and I
don't send any emails. I don't want people to be like, yo,
bro, I joined your email list and I'm not heard from you. So
it makes sense to have some kind of autoresponder. An
autoresponder is a fancy way of saying automation. So if we
think about any of the ways that I collect people's emails,
I want the first seven, 14, 20, or 25, or even 30 emails to
be automated so that when someone signs up, I can chill, I
can relax. And I know that person's getting nurtured with
well-curated emails. So for you guys to consider whatever
business, whatever niche you're in, maybe accounting, maybe
jujitsu, maybe you're a gym owner, maybe you're in CrossFit,
maybe you're even in business to business. There is a rife
and prime opportunity right in front of you to then create
an automation. So the second someone signs up, they get hit
One of the first ones that I joined was from a guy called

business. And at the end of that, he got me to buy his book.
Now his sales funnel is actually amazing because he would
have spent and paid ads, I don't know, maybe $7 in acquiring
me to sign up to his email list. And then I would have gone
through 52 days, 52 ways, whatever. And then I ended up
spending $15 on his book. So he's getting a row as return on
ad spend or potentially double. So when we look to creating
these automations, creating these nurtures, creating these
flows, ask yourself, do you want that first point of contact
to be manual or do you want it to be automated? If you want
it to be automated, look into choosing a platform that's got
a good, solid autoresponder function. I didn't do this when
I started email marketing about what, eight, nine years ago.
And at the time I was single, I was living at home or I was
traveling Australia, waking up in the morning, having my
breakfast, writing an email, that was fine. It was something
I could do every day and I did it for years. And in some

alternatives. So consider what's best for you. What do you

=== PT Starter Kit / In-Person Assessments ===

So when you first start working with someone, probably in
the consult, you're going to talk to them a little bit about
their goals, tell them a little bit about kind of the things
that you want to do. There's going to have to be some kind
of in-person assessment. So often if your gym is a
functional training room, go in there. First thing I get
people to do is I go, can you sit in a squat for me? They
go, okay. Someone's mobility to sit in a squat is going to
tell you a lot about that person, whether they can sit,
whether they can't, whether they can get to depth, whether
they can't. You can then say, okay, cool, sit in a squat. 90
% of people are going to find that really awkward. You go,
cool. This is very difficult. What I'm going to do is I'm
going to get you to raise your heels. We used to have like a
battle rope in the functional training room. I go, put your
heels on that rope, now squat down. They'd get much deeper.
I go, cool. I said, what we're doing here is I'm probably
going to elevate your heel to get you to squat better. I go,
we could spend months of mobilizing the ankle. I said, or I
could just raise your heels. I go, this is going to
artificially create mobility in your ankle, permitting you
to squat deeper. You go, oh, that's interesting. Aha moment,
remember? Then I'd say, okay, let's do 10 squats. I want you
to go as deep as you feel comfortable, just body weight with
your feet up on the battle rope. Cool. Do 10. Say, how hard
was that? If they were like eight, nine, I go, sweet. This
person's not touching a weight today. I'd say to that
person, okay, cool. If they go off four out of 10, I'll go,
okay, you're pretty strong. This time we're going to do 10,
one and a quarter squats. They go, okay, what's that? You're
going to squat all the way down to the bottom, come up a
quarter, go back down to the bottom, come back up. They do
that and they'll be like, oh Jesus, pretty sore. How hard
was that? They go, eight. I go, cool. I go, that's just a
demonstration of me telling you that I can make things
harder in here without having to give you weights. We have a
lot of time potentially training together. If you choose to
do personal training, I just want to show you there that
there are many ways. We can manipulate the body without me
having to touch you, stretch you, whatever, and make your
life easier. You'll notice that this exercise here is
predominantly working the front of the legs. They go, I can
feel it. I go, cool. We're going to leave that alone. We can
come back to it. Now I'm just going to see if you can hip
hinge. And we'd say, you know, have you ever done a Romanian
deadlift? You ever done this? You've had a back pain? Tell
you about it. And then we'd give them the cue for doing a
hip hinge. I would often say, okay, stand where you are.
Take your knees off lock. Now I would say to them, imagine
there's an invisible button on that wall. I want you to put
your hands behind your head. Now I want you to press that
button with your butt. And they would hip hinge and I'd go
keep your chest proud. Cool. Now I want you to go back and
press that button until you feel a stretch in your
hamstrings. I go, cool. What we're doing now is we're doing
a hip hinge. We are offsetting your butt back.

=== PT Starter Kit / Programme Phases ===

this is a very simple concept but when you communicate this
to your clients they're going to think you're a genius
imagine there is a pyramid in front of me right now when we
start a client in the onset we are going to start in a phase
that we call volume volume and intensity sit at different
ends of the spectrum intensity is the top of the pyramid
volume is the bottom so when clients start with us their rep
ranges are going to be high and they're going to be high
because we are not going to give them mad amounts of
intensity we're not going to give them mad amounts of
intensity because we don't know what they are capable of so
they are probably going to be leg pressing 10 to 15 reps
bicep curling 10 to 15 reps mostly everything 10 to 15 reps
and we say to our clients hey just to let you know for the
first four weeks we are in an accumulation phase an
accumulation phase means we are getting a lot of volume
because we want to get motor patterns we want people to get
used to the movements whether it's a lateral raise whatever
it is then the next four weeks keep them excited we go hey
we're building up the intensity they go what does that mean
we go we're going to the 8 to 12 rep range it could even be
the same exercises but you might want to tinker them a
little bit so they feel like they're getting the value for
money and you say to them hey we're going to start lifting
heavier they go why because our reps are coming down we are
working to an intensity phase then the next four weeks after

the lift gamma gain and offset wheels. Now to simplify this
for you I'm going to compare each of these adjustments to
shadows mid-tones highlights and general exposure. So for
example the lift gamma will increase the darkest points of
the image gamma will increase the mid-tones of the image and
the gain will affect the highlights of the image and then
the offset will affect the general exposure of the image.
Now I do have to make this clear these are not the exact
same as shadows mid-tones and highlights as we've actually
got specific adjustments for that in the log wheels down
below. However in order for you to understand how they work
you can compare them to shadows mid-tones highlights. The
key difference however is the lift gamma and gain
adjustments are a little bit more of a softer adjustment.
That affects the image on a global scale. Shadows mid-tones
and highlights are more specific and sharper adjustments.
Generally using the lift gamma and gain is a better option
when trying to create your desired exposure. So we're going
to reset this adjustment here by clicking this icon and
we'll now go in and we'll make the adjustments we want to
make. I'm going to raise up the gain like so bring down the

it also lets us know if we're pushing our adjustments too
far. So if we remove this adjustment here and then we turn

waveform. This is showing us that there is not much
contrast. By adding in that CST and exposure we can see that
we've stretched that image over a wider spectrum of exposure
bringing in more highlights and gain creating a more
balanced and contrasted image. Now if I was to push my gain
up too high like so you can see that the image starts to
flatten at the top of the scope and that is represented in
our image over here as being too bright or overexposed. The
technical term for this is clipping, highlight clipping. So
our highlights here are losing detail. Once the highlights
go past 90 to 100 it begins to flatten out and we lose that
information. So it's very important when you're colour
grading or colour correcting that you ensure the highlights
are safely below these numbers. So let's bring that back
down again like so making sure we're keeping this ideally
spot to be safe like so. Alternatively our shadows can also
get too dark and we can lose information in the shadows
which the technical term for this is crushing the shadows.
So now you can see here it's flat lined and in our image

So again we want to ensure that when we're grading that we

=== Black Belt Content Mastery / Editing Walkthroughs: DaVinci Resolve ===

Hi guys, my name is Declan and I'm James' videographer and
video editor and today I'm going to be giving you a quick
run-through about how we use DaVinci Resolve to edit James'
videos. So first things first, I want you to go into DaVinci
Resolve. When you open the program, you'll be greeted with
this window here, which is the Project Manager. First, we're
going to go down to the bottom right-hand corner, press New
Project, and we'll name this Tutorial. Okay, so when you
open up DaVinci, you'll be greeted with this screen here,
and I want you to pay attention to these little icons down
the bottom. You're going to notice seven icons, okay? These
are the different tabs within the software. Each tab is
responsible for a different task. The first tab is called
the Media tab, and this is where we're going to organize all
our files. The second tab is the Cut tab, which is great for
speed editing long sections of dialogue or making quick cuts
to your edit. The next tab is the Edit tab, and this is
where we'll spend the majority of our time. We'll construct
the edit, add music, do basic effects, and then we'll go on
to the next tab, which is the Fusion tab. This is a little
bit more advanced. This is where we'll do more advanced.
We'll do more advanced motion graphics, 3D compositing, but
we won't really cover this page in this tutorial. And then
we've got the Color tab. This is where we'll do color
correction and color grading of our footage. Next up, we've
got the Fairlight tab. This is where we'll do audio
processing. So a great tool that I'm going to show you later
is called Voice Isolation, which is going to help to remove
unwanted background noise, and I'll explain that later in
the tutorial. And then finally, we have the Export tab,
which is where we're going to export our videos for social
media or YouTube. Okay, so we're going to start in the Media
tab. And the first thing we're going to do is create some...
new folders. In DaVinci, folders are called bins. So when I
press right click, new bin. We're going to name this bin
Sony FX3. Then we'll create another bin. We'll name this
Sony A7 IV. And then we'll create one more bin, Osmo. So
I've created these bins in order to organize our footage.
Depending on what you're editing, you may be shooting with
multiple cameras. You may be shooting different scenes,
different days, different subjects. A really helpful tip is
to organize all this. You may want to organize your footage
into these bins before you start editing, which will make it
much easier to find your footage when it comes to the edit.
So we're going to go into Sony FX3 folder. We're going to
press Command I. We're going to locate the footage that we
want to add, which is in this folder here. Drag it all in
and click Open. Now you're going to get a message here that
says Change Project Frame Rate. I want you to press Change.
What that's going to do is it's going to make sure that the
timeline matches the footage that you imported. So the frame
rate will be the same. That's all we need to know for now.
Okay. As you can see, we've got our FX3. We've got our FX3
video files in the folder. Then we'll scroll down to the
Sony A7IV. Again, pressing Command I. And we'll navigate to
the Sony A7IV folder. We'll then drag in all the footage and
click Open. And finally, go to the Osmo bin. Now another way
you can import the footage is go up to the top, File,
Import, Media. And that will bring us back to the same
folder. Navigate to the Osmo folder, find the clip, and
Open. Okay, fantastic. So as you'll notice... Down the

Sony A7IV clips, and we've got Osmo clips here, which is

=== Silver Play Button / Content Ideation Fundamentals ===

Let me tell you about the most embarrassing thing I see
business owners do on YouTube. They watch Alex Hormozzi,
they see a video that gets 2 million views and they think,
right, exact title and thumbnail, I'll just copy that. But
here's why you're never going to get views if you try and
use this strategy. Because let's say you've got this
accountant from Birmingham and he's called Dave. Dave sees
Hormozzi's video with a tweet screenshot in the thumbnail.
Dave copies it exactly, uses the same title, format. But
here's the problem. Dave has 47 Twitter followers and runs a
local accounting practice 10 minutes outside Solihull. So
here's a question for you. When YouTube shows both videos on
the homepage, which one do you think people are going to
click? The one from the guy who just did a $100 million book
launch with a team of a thousand people? Or Dave from
Birmingham who's never told a story in his life? And this is
where 99% of business channels are failing with the
ideation. They try and compete in a red ocean against people
like Hormozzi, Cody Sanchez, Dan Martel. Creators have been
around for decades with massive teams and endless
credibility. And you're never going to win that fight. But
here's what Dave should have done instead. And it's exactly
what I'm going to show you to do to reliably find video
ideas that you can put into action that won't come across as
cringe. Like copying another Alex Hormozzi vid. You know
you've done it. I know you've done it. Stop it. I've done
it. Finding viral video ideas is literally the most
important thing you can do to grow on YouTube. Once you've

Now that you know the thumbnail formats that you can use,

is what we call the mobile test. And this is the test that
kills 90% of thumbnails. Can you read everything clearly on
a phone screen? Most people design thumbnails on their
laptop like I just did then, and then wonder why nobody
clicks, but 70% of YouTube views still happen on mobile. So

=== Silver Play Button / Hooks ===

The key to writing a good hook is something we can steal
from Hollywood. What do I mean by that? Right, imagine it's
1am and you're watching Insidious and it gets to the really
quiet part of the film. You're not feeling too scared,
everything seems kind of peaceful, and then this happens. I
can still hear that voice.
This is exactly how hooks work on social media. They wake
people up from their sleepwalking trance on the algorithm.
Think about it like this. Most videos have slow, boring
hooks and people scroll past them. The audience doesn't want
to watch your video and it doesn't make sales. It's not the
quiet part of a horror film. But then 5% of videos have
hooks that make you sit up and pay attention. It's a bit
like a jump scare in a horror movie. Immediately your heart
is racing, you have a flood of emotion, your eyes are glued
to the movie. You're like, these are what I call jump
scares. Hooks, and when you use these in your videos, your
audience, they're actually emotionally invested. They're
listening to what you say. Just like getting someone's
attention in a horror movie. And when you have your
audience's attention, you can sell to them and you can
actually convert them and you can get them to want to
listen, to hear to your offer. So how do you actually write
one of these hooks? There are three easy ways. To do it,
they work like this. In the simplest form, a jump scare hook
is about saying and or showing someone that produces a spike
of emotion in a viewer. This could be fear, excitement,
optimism, anger. And the worst thing you can really do here
is to be boring. So there are going to be four jump scare
hook types you can steal to create some excitement in your
viewer. The first one is found in the hook to this video.
I'm sure you've realized ever since the pandemic that
absolutely everyone you've ever met has now got a podcast.
And this is not even plugged into anything. But there is a
big problem on the horizon. That we're already starting to
experience. This is called a contrarian hook. This is where
you say something most people agree with. For instance, most
people do have a podcast. They've been told it's a good way
to make money. And then I disagree with it. I use this all
the time. For example, in this video, there are so many
gurus online, especially on YouTube, telling personal
trainers, if you want to go online, work from Bali remote,
make $15,000 a month, then just follow these steps. But
there's a big issue that no one's really talking about. All
of these gurus have made all of their money, not from
fitness businesses, they made their money from selling
coaches the dream. No sales calls, selling DMs. You don't
even need a sales funnel. Is to identify the common beliefs
held by my avatar and then finding the ones I disagree with
and then hooking the viewer with your uncommon belief. The
key is it has to be contrarian. Not just running doesn't
help you build muscle, try and create something your viewers
never heard of before, which brings us to the next jump
scare hook you can use. See if you can spot where it is

=== Silver Play Button / Making More Money ===

You've probably seen these videos all over your YouTube
homepage. Some creator with 5,000 subscribers getting 900
views per video and they're making an absolute killing. 20k,
30k, sometimes 50k a month. Meanwhile, there's another
creator with 100,000 subscribers, millions of views a month,
and they're barely scraping by. And you think, how the fuck
is that possible? I'll tell you exactly how. I've worked
with some clients making over a quarter of a million dollars
a year with a few hundred thousand views. I know someone
making 10 to 40k a month with 10,000 views, and these people
aren't lucky. They've just figured out something most
creators never learn, and that's what I'm trying to hammer
into you. Making more money doesn't require you to chase
mega views or go viral. It's about alignment. So let me show
you what I mean. Two creators, same niche, same view count.
Let's say they both get 10,000 views on a video. Person A
makes content about how to make money online. Audience is
students, side hustlers, people who know money, because they
are speaking about such general things. One video is about
websites, the next is about becoming a freelancer, the next
is about making money with dropshipping. They can't sell an
offer to this audience despite getting DCDs. Person B makes
content about how to make money online as a freelance
copywriter. Then every video they make is target towards how
to become a freelance copywriter, how to find clients, how
to deliver for clients, how to use AI to save hours in the
copywriting process. And the result is person B can sell a
two grand offer and make hundreds of sales each year from a
modest amount of views. Same views, but a completely
different bank account balance. And if we ask ourselves why,
it's because creator B has something called alignment. Their
positioning, their content, their offer all points to the
same person with the same problem. Creator A is all over the
place, broad content, wrong audience, and they can never
create an offer that matches something so general. So let me
show you the alignment framework that determines whether you
make zero or 30k from the same amount of views. It's called
the PP method. Reminds me of my time in Thailand, co-PP. Ah,
big boy. Anyway, moving swiftly on. P1, problem. What pain
point does your content address? Because your content needs
to be about one specific painful problem. Some bad examples
that are too broad could be how to grow on YouTube, how to
lose weight, or how to make money online. Good examples
could be specific. How to get your first 1,000 subscribers
as a business coach. How to lose 20 pounds when you work a
corporate desk job and have no time. Or number three, how to
make money online with SMMA, or dropshipping, or e-commerce
in the food and beverage brand. When you address one problem
for one person, people are much more likely to invest in
your help, to pay to solve that problem faster or easier. So
how do you find this problem? It's pretty simple. All it is
is solving the problem either you've solved for yourself or
that you've sold for clients. Then you make. All your
content about different angles of that same problem. Unlike
what you might have heard before, you probably don't need to
target a super specific person if you're niching around a
specific problem. That's likely enough. I always say niche
the problem, not the person. So rather than me saying, oh, I
want to work with mums, and someone says, why? Oh, they're
tired, and they never put themselves first, and they've got
a bad sleep pattern. We could help nurses with the exact
same solution. So instead, you would niche in on women that
don't put themselves first, and that have terrible sleep.
And then it could be women, it could be mums, it could be
other people that work night shifts, whatever it is. Then we
have the second P, P2, product. And this is where most
people fuck it up. They've got the problem right, and
they've got the person right, but their offer doesn't match.
So here would be some examples of misalignment. So the
problem could be how to get a six pack when you're over 40.
The person could be men aged 40 to 50 in a corporate desk
job that don't really have any time. The offer, a 50 pound
ebook with generic meal plans. Does that work? I mean,

because a 40 year old professional with the desk job could

he's willing to pay for more and proper support. And the
basic rule of thumb is that your offer should be the exact
solution to the problem that your content talks about. We've

There are seven design mistakes I see come up all the time
with thumbnails that makes them look completely amateur. And
if your thumbnails look amateur, you're never going to get
views and sales. But really, these seven things all come
down to just one principle that I want you to think about.
Does this design of the thumbnail make the image look clear
and readable? That's it. That's the only rule you need to
think about. So in this video, I want to show you the seven
ways people break this rule with their design, and I've
organized it into what I call the method. You'll see why in
a second. So to show you exactly how this method works so
that you can avoid making these same design mistakes for
yourself, I'm going to use one of James's thumbnails and
remake it with these errors so that you know how to spot
them. Now, this is one of my favorite thumbnails that James

incredible for the business channel because it also brought
in over five figures in sales, just one video alone. Now, it
follows most of these design rules to a T. And for that
reason, although it looks really simple, the image is also
incredibly clear and understandable to grasp, right? But let

rules and how you fix them, starting with the first C in our
method. Now, what do you think of this version of the
thumbnail where we put James's eyes at the bottom of the
frame? Now, compare this with the original where his eyes
sit at the top line of this kind of grid that you can see.
This one is way better, right? And that's because it uses
something called the rule of thirds. And this rule creates a
natural feeling of balance within your image. And this is
the first C of design, composition. Now, our eyes are
naturally drawn to these kind of intersection points on the
grid. So when you place your subject's eyes, you place some
text or an object at these points of intersection, the
thumbnail feels way more professional, but also it's a lot
clearer to instantly read. And how can you do this for
yourself? Well, in Photoshop, you can turn on these lines by
hitting view, guides, new guide layout, and then hitting OK.
Then you just want to line up your items in the frame on
this grid. This brings us onto the next C of design. So for
a second, think about whenever you're reading a book. In the
West, we read from left to right, right? But look what
happens if we flip the text to the other side of the
thumbnail in James's image. Now, look, it's not impossible
to read, but it takes a heck of a lot longer to understand
than if we put the text on the left. And when your viewers

a country where you read from right to left, in which case,
